challenges.question: Can a decision be legal but still be unethical?
challenges.situation: A shop legally raises the price of drinking water bottles by 300% during a flood, when there is no other water available nearby.
challenges.counterargument: Some argue that if a law allows something, judging it as 'unethical' is just personal opinion. Prices respond to demand, and high prices may even stop people from buying more than they need.

challenges.question: Does having more information always lead to better decisions?
challenges.situation: Before choosing a college course, Kiran reads 200 online reviews, watches 40 videos and joins 12 groups — and still cannot decide.
challenges.counterargument: More information can confuse rather than clarify, especially if it is low quality or conflicting. Knowing what information matters may be more important than having more.

challenges.question: Is a popular opinion necessarily a reliable opinion?
challenges.situation: A poll in your class shows 85% of students believe a certain diet makes you smarter.
challenges.counterargument: Popular opinions often reflect shared experience, and dismissing them can be arrogant. When many independent people agree, that agreement can carry some weight.

challenges.question: Can treating everyone equally sometimes produce unfair outcomes?
challenges.situation: A sports day rule says every student must run the same 400 metres to earn a participation certificate, including students with injuries or disabilities.
challenges.counterargument: Adjusting rules for some people can feel like favouritism and may make achievements seem less meaningful. Equal rules are transparent and easy to check.

challenges.question: Should people be held responsible for sharing information they believed was true but did not verify?
challenges.situation: Sam forwards a message about a 'free laptop scheme' that turns out to be a scam. Several classmates lose money after clicking the link.
challenges.counterargument: Sam acted in good faith and did not intend harm. Expecting everyone to verify everything is unrealistic — the scammer is the one truly responsible.

challenges.question: Is an environmentally friendly product always the most sustainable choice?
challenges.situation: Alex replaces a working plastic water bottle with a new steel one every few months because of new designs.
challenges.counterargument: Encouraging people to buy green products creates demand that drives companies to change. Even imperfect green choices push the market in the right direction.

challenges.question: When should loyalty give way to fairness?
challenges.situation: Your team captain, a close friend, selects only their friends for a college tournament, leaving out a stronger player.
challenges.counterargument: Teams that trust each other play better together. Loyalty and friendship can be legitimate reasons, not just bias.

challenges.question: What evidence would convince you to change a strongly held opinion?
challenges.situation: Think of an opinion you hold strongly — about food, technology, education or anything else.
challenges.counterargument: Some say strong opinions should not change easily; constantly changing your mind can make you seem unreliable or easily influenced.

challenges.question: Is it ever right to break a rule?
challenges.situation: A hostel rule says the gate closes at 9 pm. At 9:15 pm, a hostel-mate needs to go to a pharmacy for urgent medicine for a friend with a high fever.
challenges.counterargument: If everyone decides for themselves when rules can be broken, rules lose their meaning. There may be an official way to get help instead.

challenges.question: Does a good intention make an action good?
challenges.situation: A volunteer group distributes old clothes in a flood-hit area. Many clothes are torn or unwashed, and some residents feel insulted.
challenges.counterargument: Judging people who try to help can discourage helping at all. Something given in kindness is better than nothing.

challenges.question: Should you always say what you honestly think?
challenges.situation: A friend shows you their first short film, which they worked hard on for months. You find it boring.
challenges.counterargument: Honest feedback helps people improve. Hiding your real opinion can be a form of disrespect.

challenges.question: Is free really free?
challenges.situation: A free photo-editing app becomes hugely popular. Its terms say it may use uploaded faces to 'improve services'.
challenges.counterargument: Users get real value at no cost, and companies need some way to earn. Most people know their data is used and accept it.

challenges.question: Should the majority always decide?
challenges.situation: A class votes 45–15 to go on a tour that costs ₹8,000 per student. Some of the 15 cannot afford it.
challenges.counterargument: Voting is the fairest way to settle group disagreements. If the minority can always block decisions, nothing will ever get done.

challenges.question: Is it fair to judge people from the past by today's values?
challenges.situation: A famous scientist from 150 years ago made great discoveries but also wrote things we now see as deeply unfair to some groups of people.
challenges.counterargument: People are shaped by their time. Judging them by values they never knew is unfair; we should judge them by the standards of their era.

challenges.question: Can technology be neutral?
challenges.situation: A photo filter app makes everyone's skin lighter by default.
challenges.counterargument: Technology is just a tool; it reflects what users choose. Developers simply follow what most users seem to want.

challenges.question: Is it better to be right or to be kind?
challenges.situation: In a group discussion, an older relative states a fact that you know is outdated. Correcting them may embarrass them in front of others.
challenges.counterargument: Letting wrong information pass means others may believe it. Respect includes trusting people to handle correction.

challenges.question: Do experts deserve more trust than ordinary people?
challenges.situation: A senior farmer's prediction about this year's monsoon differs from the weather department's forecast.
challenges.counterargument: Local, experience-based knowledge can capture patterns that scientific models miss. Experts have also been wrong many times.

challenges.question: Should you help someone who doesn't ask for help?
challenges.situation: A classmate is clearly struggling to carry many books while using crutches, but has not asked anyone.
challenges.counterargument: Offering help that wasn't requested can feel patronising and suggest the person is not capable.

challenges.question: Is one person's action meaningless against a big problem?
challenges.situation: Ash stops using single-use plastic. A friend says, 'One person won't make any difference to global pollution.'
challenges.counterargument: Large problems are driven by industries and governments. Focusing on individual habits can distract from the system changes that really matter.

challenges.question: Is silence a choice?
challenges.situation: In a meeting, someone makes a mocking comment about a colleague's accent. Everyone laughs or stays quiet.
challenges.counterargument: Not every situation requires a response; speaking up in public can escalate conflict or embarrass the person further.

challenges.question: Should marks be the main measure of learning?
challenges.situation: Robin scores 92% by memorising answers but cannot explain the main ideas to a friend.
challenges.counterargument: Marks are objective, comparable and fair to all. Other measures of learning can be vague and biased.
